newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Storm cuts water in some New Zealand areas.
newsitem.headline: Storm cuts water in some New Zealand areas.

text.p: Water supplies in northern parts of New Zealand were cut or contaminated on Tuesday after the remnants of Cyclone Fergus lashed the country on Monday, a civil defence spokesman said.
A state of emergency covering the North Island's Coromandel Peninsula, east of Auckland, was expected to be lifted later in the day as the storm lost intensity.

Civil Defence spokesman Adrian Catran said water supplies were lost completely because of a blocked intake at the resort town of Pauanui, on the east coast of the Coromandel, and the nearby town of Whitianga's water supply was contaminated.
"We're working desperately of course to get...water back on to those areas. We've got water flowing into the reservoir at Whitianga but the next 10 to 12 hours are critical," Catran said.
He said civil defence staff hoped to supply water to Pauanui for 15 minutes every two hours, but it should be used only if absolutely necessary.

A state of emergency was imposed in the region on Monday and thousands of visitors to the peninsula had their holiday plans disrupted after heavy rain and strong winds lashed the area. Roads were closed and holidaymakers fled camping grounds as rain fell at the rate of 34 mm (1.3 inches) per hour.
Meteorologists downgraded Fergus from a cyclone to a "very deep depression" as it bore down on New Zealand, but it still brought torrential rain and wind gusts of up to 130 km/hour (80 miles/hour).
Floods closed major roads and high winds felled trees and brought down power and telephone lines in some areas.
However, despite a thorough dousing and isolated wind damage, the storm was not as intense or as widespread as predicted. Heavy rain and high winds were no longer expected over the country.

Orchardists and farmers in the eastern North Island's Hawkes Bay escaped relatively unscathed after the storm lost intensity overnight. Farmers without irrigation said the rain was welcome, breaking a drought.
"It's pretty much all downhill from here, I think," Meteorological Service chief meteorologist Augie Auer told Auckland radio.
